headline: Forecasters tracked quiet, frosty October weather, then watched a stormy pattern build into a damaging wind and surf event on November 7.
summary:
Early on, the forecasts were about cold, dry autumn weather. On Oct 9 and 10 forecasters issued the season's first Frost Advisories. A weak atmospheric river (a narrow stream of moisture) was expected to aim mostly at British Columbia, and the midweek rain kept shrinking. A warm spell with high pressure aloft was forecast for Thursday and Friday, Oct 15 and 16. Forecasters held to that call. They trimmed the peak warmth on Oct 12, from over 10 degrees above normal to 5 to 10 degrees above. They also split a possibly strong weekend storm into two weaker systems with a low risk of damaging winds. From Oct 17 through Oct 22 the outlook stayed mostly dry and cool, with fog and frost chances. The weekend system around Oct 24 and 25 was repeatedly called a toss-up, with models split on its track. By Oct 22 the first early hints of a more active pattern for late October and early November appeared. Forecasters labeled them early signals, not firm predictions.

The first real weather impact in the forecasts was mountain snow. On Oct 25 forecasters called the Tuesday night to Wednesday front the season's first noticeable Cascade snow event, with very uneven snow odds from pass to pass. By Oct 26 a Winter Weather Advisory was issued, and pass-by-pass totals followed, up to about 3 inches at Snoqualmie. By Oct 28 the advisory had expired and snow had faded a lot, with most falling in and around Mount Rainier. Then the cold took over. A Freeze Watch for parts of southwest Washington on Oct 29 became a Freeze Warning on Oct 30. A Frost Advisory was added for areas north of Seattle, and a Dense Fog Advisory including Seattle covered early Sunday, Nov 1. Forecasters later backed off Monday's fog to patchy fog or low cloud.

The pattern shift toward wet and windy weather became firmer in early November. On Nov 2 forecasters pointed to a strong storm late Thursday into Friday, with about a 50% chance of damaging gusts. On Nov 3 they pushed the active pattern back, to a weak front Wednesday evening into Thursday, with the stronger storms starting Friday. They gave 40 to 80% odds of gusts over 40 mph on the coast and north of Admiralty Inlet, and noted that leafy trees raise the risk of power outages. By Nov 5 Wind Advisories were in effect for Friday. The bigger concern moved to a second, stronger front on Saturday night.

As of Nov 7, forecasters expect a strong cold front tonight into Sunday morning. A High Wind Warning covers the coast, with a 50 to 70% chance of gusts over 55 mph. A Wind Advisory covers interior lowlands including Seattle, with gusts of 45 to 50 mph at times. A High Surf Warning calls for waves of 22 to 28 feet. Forecasters give a 20 to 30% chance of coastal thunderstorms, and 10 to 20% inland. Showers and falling snow levels follow on Sunday. More rain comes Monday and through midweek, with further systems late in the week. Forecasters call the model guidance for next week "a bit shaky" on timing and strength. No river flooding is expected in the next seven days, but repeated rain will soak the ground and could matter for later storms.
